content.page_title: Timing of revascularization; Balloons and stents (excerpt)
content.summary: Guidance on timing of revascularization in ACS and comparative outcomes of stent types and drug-coated balloon (DCB) angioplasty.
key_points: IRA physiology: The infarct-related artery (IRA) may underestimate true haemodynamic severity of coronary stenosis; beyond 1 week from the acute event, fractional flow reserve (FFR) measurement can reliably predict abnormal nuclear imaging.

Timing of revascularization (9.1.3): In some ACS patients undergoing invasive coronary angiography (ICA) an initial conservative strategy with optimized guideline-directed medical therapy may be considered case-by-case (examples: small-calibre vessels, occluded small side branch, concerns about antithrombotic non-compliance). For complex CAD/anticipated complex PCI, initial conservative strategy in medically stabilized, asymptomatic patients allows Heart Team discussion.
Balloons and stents (9.1.4): New-generation drug-eluting stents (DES) are associated with superior safety and improved efficacy versus bare-metal stents (BMS) and first-generation DES.
- NORSTENT: largest trial comparing new-generation DES vs BMS; primary endpoint (death or MI) comparable between groups, but DES reduced target lesion revascularization (TLR) and stent thrombosis.
- COMFORTABLE-AMI and EXAMINATION: reported clinical superiority of DES over BMS for lower rates of re-infarction, TLR, and stent thrombosis; benefits persisted at longer-term follow-up.
Drug-coated balloon (DCB) strategy: DCB angioplasty without stenting has been proposed for NSTE-ACS but evidence is limited.

- REVELATION (single-centre, prospective randomized): compared paclitaxel-coated balloon angioplasty vs DES PCI in acute MI; in 120 patients undergoing PPCI, primary endpoint (target vessel FFR at 9 months) was not significantly different.

- PEPCAD NSTEMI (small randomized): 210 patients compared DCB with provisional stenting (BMS or DES); mean follow-up 9.2 months showed DCB non-inferior to stent for primary endpoint (target lesion failure rate 3.8% vs 6.6%, P = 0.53).
Limitations: Many DCB studies are small and underpowered; further investigation is required before changing guideline recommendations for use of DCB in NSTE-ACS.
recommendations: Consider initial conservative management in selected ACS patients undergoing ICA when appropriate (small vessels, occluded side branch, concerns about antithrombotic adherence).
Use of new-generation DES is generally preferred over BMS given reduced TLR and stent thrombosis and preserved long-term benefit.
DCB angioplasty without stenting may be considered investigational in NSTE-ACS; larger trials needed to inform guideline recommendations.

trials_mentioned.name: NORSTENT
trials_mentioned.notes: Largest clinical trial comparing new-generation DES vs BMS; primary endpoint death or MI comparable; DES reduced TLR and stent thrombosis.

trials_mentioned.name: COMFORTABLE-AMI
trials_mentioned.notes: Compared biolimus-eluting erodible stent coating vs bare-metal stents in ST-elevation MI; reported superiority of DES over BMS.

trials_mentioned.name: EXAMINATION
trials_mentioned.notes: Everolimus-eluting stents vs bare-metal stents in ST-elevation MI; showed clinical superiority of DES.

trials_mentioned.name: REVELATION
trials_mentioned.notes: Randomized single-centre trial comparing paclitaxel-coated balloon angioplasty vs DES PCI in acute MI (120 patients); no significant difference in target vessel FFR at 9 months.

trials_mentioned.name: PEPCAD NSTEMI
trials_mentioned.notes: Randomized trial (210 patients) comparing DCB with provisional stenting in non-ST-elevation MI; DCB non-inferior over mean 9.2 months follow-up but sample size limited.
